newsitem.title: HUNGARY: MOL WANTS PRODUCER GAS HIKE NEAR 18.8 PCT.
newsitem.headline: MOL WANTS PRODUCER GAS HIKE NEAR 18.8 PCT.

text.p: Hungarian oil and gas company MOL Rt said on Thursday it expected to be allowed to raise the producer price of gas in January by a margin close to the recently announced consumer price rise of 18.8 percent
"We hope that something close to the figure (of 18.8 percent) will be the actual price increase for MOL as well," MOL director Zoltan Aldott told a Budapest conference on Hungary's capital markets.
The government announced last month that it would raise gas prices to domestic consumers by 18.8 percent and electricity prices by 24.9 percent on January 1.

However, it did not specify how the energy companies would share extra funds from the increases. The Hungarian Energy Office said the government is not likely to announce the details until mid-December.
Aldott said a producer price hike near 18.8 percent would generate healthy operating profits for MOL in 1997. "With (such a rise) a substantial swing in operating profitability will happen," he said.
Hungary promised foreign investors to which it sold large chunks of energy companies in 1995 they would be assured an eight percent profit margin for the energy sector from 1997.
MOL was also given the same undertaking.

However analysts fear that in order to ensure such margins for investors such as Gaz de France and Italgaz who have bought into the regional gas distribution network, MOL, their exclusive supplier, may be forced to accept producer price increases substantially below 18.8 percent.
Aldott said MOL hoped it would receive a similar price increase to those of the gas distribution companies
"Between the gas distribution companies and MOL, no-one should be getting worse treatment fron the government point of view," he said.

He also hoped that the new pricing mechanism would allow more frequent adjustments in price in view of Hungary's relatively high inflation (currently around 24 percent) and the crawling peg system of devaluing the forint (by 1.2 percent per month).
"(With inflation and devaluation) one thing is sure: that dollar-denominated gas imports will go up, and we hope regular adjustment will be possible," he said.
MOL imports almost of the gas it supplies to Hungary from Russia, for which it pays world market prices.
Aldott told Reuters that he hoped quarterly price increases would be possible.
"A monthly basis would be hard to handle and we have a major supply contract with Russia whereby the price is based on a quarterly adjustment," he said.

Aldott added that following discussions with the government's energy comminssioner Imre Karl, MOL hoped that the there would be an increase in the types of costs included in the pricing mechanism upon which the profit margin was calculated.
"At the moment costs such as environmental measures are not included," he said. "We think they could be in the future."
He also appealed to the government to close the gap in price between domestic production and more expensive imported energy.
"The value of Hungarian production is much lower than the import price," he said. "Gradually we hope that it will be taken at the same value as imports," he said.
MOL shares closed up 25 at 1,850 forints on Thursday on the Budapest Stock Exchange.
